title: How I built a 500k-Domain Search Engine for Makers in a Weekend for $10
content_html:
marlin

Sunday, 2am. I couldn’t sleep and I was annoyed at search engines again. Every query I actually cared about, portfolios, zines, weird little art projects, one-person software, drowned under a foot of corporate documentation and SEO sludge. So I did the thing you do at 2am: I opened a terminal and typed out a plan.

“I want to make a search engine for myself only. There are 40-ish million domains. We can store a bit of metadata about each one. Even with 1KB each that’s 40GB, which is doable.”

By Wednesday lunch I had 560,183 homepages catalogued, an empty queue of anything worth fetching next, and a decision to stop. This is the story of that weekend: what I built, what broke, what it cost, and what I’d tell you if you wanted to build your own.

The headline, if you only read one paragraph: for about $10, an overnight GPU rental, and a few hours of steering the thing while it ran, you can have a personal search index of a few hundred thousand sites, under a gigabyte on disk. That’s the whole pitch. Everything below is how I got there and where the sharp edges are.

Full technical details are provided separately.

What I was actually trying to build

Not “index the web.” Just: find people doing stuff, art, code, hardware, poetry, little theatres, and not drown in docs.company.com. Personal, single user, no accounts. A crawler that only ever looks at homepages, a small local language model that reads each one and writes a name, two or three sentences, a category, and a handful of tags. A little search UI on top with fuzzy matching so I could type half a word and still find the right site.

I wrote down what I was explicitly not building, mostly so that agents helping me wouldn’t quietly “simplify” it into something bigger: no IP scanning, no Redis, no storing full page HTML, no recrawl scheduler, nothing multi-tenant. Ignore was just a checkbox on a category, applied at search time. The crawler still summarised ecommerce sites, I just didn’t have to look at them.

The napkin math was tens of millions of domains at roughly 1KB of metadata each, which is genuinely nothing for a Postgres box. Page text itself was never meant to be a corpus, just a scratch buffer that gets thrown away the moment the model is done with it.

The machine

Four processes, three of them on my own PC, one rented GPU that never touches the database directly:

  • A fetcher. Grabs a pending domain, tries HTTPS then HTTP, pulls the title, body text, and outbound links with a simple HTML parser, no JavaScript execution. Sets the row to “ready.”
  • A worker. Grabs a ready domain, skips the model entirely if the page is empty, parked, or a bot-challenge wall, otherwise makes one structured request to a small local model (Gemma, 4B parameters) and gets back a name, summary, category, and tags. Wipes the scratch text, enqueues the outbound links at a priority based on what kind of page they came from.
  • A steward. This one doesn’t touch the main queue at all. It samples domains from hosts that are producing suspiciously many pages, asks the model “block, keep, or unsure,” and quietly maintains a blocklist. More on why I needed this later.
  • An API and a tiny web UI. Search with filters, a page to toggle which categories are hidden, and a dashboard so I could actually see what the factory was doing instead of squinting at logs.

Everything the fetcher grabs lives directly on the domain’s own database row while it’s “in progress.” Once the model is done with it, that text gets wiped. That matters more than it sounds, because at any real scale you cannot let raw page text pile up forever. Forty million rows times a few kilobytes each adds up fast, and I only needed that text for the few seconds the model was reading it.

The web is 90% corporate, actually

The first version worked within a couple hours. Point it at a sample of domains, watch things get summarised, search for them. Great. Then, Sunday afternoon, I looked at what had actually been catalogued and it was the wrong web. Over 90% corporate sites and documentation. My seed list was skewed and the crawler had no opinions about what to chase next.

The fix wasn’t to block anything. Blocking felt tempting but wrong, because a boring corporate docs page might still link out to someone’s personal blog, and I didn’t want to lose that. Instead I weighted the queue: pages classified as “portfolio” or “zine” or “software” push their outbound links way up the priority list, pages classified as “corporate” or “docs” push theirs down. One text file, category-priority.txt, became the steering wheel for the rest of the weekend. I’d tune a number, watch what came in over the next hour, tune again.

That same afternoon I wiped the database twice because the quality was bad enough to just start over. Two bugs stood out:

One site’s summary field just said “academic-profile,” a category label the model had shoved into the wrong slot. Fix: treat a suspiciously short summary as a failure and retry once with a stricter prompt.

Another site, a GoDaddy domain-parking page with basically no real HTML, got summarised by the model as being “for the furry community.” but it had just seen the word “furry” in the hostname, with empty body, and invented an entire fandom site out of nothing. That one taught me the actual rule: trust visible text over the title, trust the title over anything guessed from the domain name, and if a page is near-empty or clearly parked, don’t even bother asking the model, just mark it and move on.

Sunday night: Tumblr is not the web

By evening the crawl had a new problem. Tumblr and Neocities blogs were showing up in such volume that they were going to become the entire index. My first instinct was to block them, which felt wrong, because Neocities specifically is exactly the aesthetic I was hunting for. The actual fix was a cap: allow the main domain always, but once a given root domain has produced more than 100 subdomains, stop enqueueing new ones from it. One pass of that rule deleted over 45,000 queued pages instantly. Tumblr still ended up contributing over 9,000 pages to the final index, since the cap only applies going forward, but it stopped being the whole story.

This was also the night the actual purpose came into focus, less “index everything,” more “find the people making things for a community.” I reseeded the crawl with about ten deliberately chosen doors: tilde communities, small independent blogging platforms, a webring or two. Almost the entire final index traces back to links found from those ten seeds, not from the seed list itself.

Monday morning brought a related flavor of the same problem: forum farms and Chinese B2B vendor microsites riding a “forum” category boost into a black hole of near-identical pages. Same lesson, different category. I demoted “forum” hard and started keeping an explicit blocklist file for known mills.

Renting a GPU, badly, then well

My own GPU, a consumer card, could summarise roughly one page per second running locally. Fine for building the prompt, hopeless for actually filling an index. So I rented a cloud GPU to run the same small model at real concurrency, and this is where most of my actual debugging time went, none of it about the AI itself.

The short version: my first rental setup used a wrapper library that insisted on spinning up a distributed compute framework even for a single GPU, and that framework fought with the host machine for CPU time. I was paying for a GPU and getting throttled by CPU contention I never asked for. Threw that away, ran the plain open source inference server instead, no wrapper. Hit a crash on cold start at high concurrency, which turned out to be a memory spike during the first batch, not a steady-state problem, fixed by ramping concurrency up gradually instead of slamming it at full speed from a cold start.

The machine that actually did the job was a mid-range workstation GPU with a full, unshared set of CPU cores attached. That distinction, a dedicated CPU slice versus an impressively named but shared one, may have mattered more than the GPU model itself. Sustained throughput on that box was around 600 summaries a minute, at a rental cost of about thirty five cents an hour. That’s roughly a dollar to catalogue a hundred thousand sites.

Ballpark napkin math at those rates, assuming you can keep the GPUs fed and they scale roughly linearly. Renting two or three GPUs costs about the same for a given milestone, because each one runs for less wall-clock time; you mostly buy days back:

Sites Approx. cost 1 GPU 2 GPUs 3 GPUs
10k ~$0.10 ~17 min ~8 min ~6 min
100k ~$1 ~3 hrs ~1.5 hrs ~1 hr
1M ~$10 ~1.2 days ~14 hrs ~9 hrs
10M ~$100 ~12 days ~6 days ~4 days

Those figures lean on the best of the three setups I actually tried. Sustained throughput across them looked like this:

* The 4090 run used the Vast.ai / vLLM wrapper with the CPU pegged — GPU underutilised. The PRO 4500 numbers are the plain vLLM setup with a dedicated CPU slice.

The GPU/CPU utilisation data came from the servers own management UI, where I noticed CPU was +90% while GPU was between 30-50%. I never benchmarked the GPU/CPU on the RTX PRO 4500 because it was an overnight run just for clearing the priority queue and wrapping things up. I got the token throughput values from the server logs. Hour by hour, the weekend looked quiet for most of Monday and Tuesday, then the good box held near 600 pages a minute until the queue was empty:

Inventing a second worker at midnight

Late Monday night, staring at the crawl still running, I asked myself something like: at this scale I can’t manually watch for bad spirals, could I have a second small process sample five, then ten, completed pages from any domain that’s producing suspiciously many, and ask the model itself whether to block it?

That became the steward, and it’s the single addition that let the index grow from around 65,000 pages to 560,000 without me babysitting it. It sat on the same local card and LM Studio I’d used for prompt work, so spiral judgements never competed with the rented GPU that was filling the index. Over the run it blocked 177 problem domains on its own, almost entirely hotel and booking mills, and correctly left alone things like universities and legitimate large platforms that just happen to have a lot of subdomains.

What the numbers actually looked like

Watching this over four days was genuinely the fun part. Early on, blogs and personal sites made up over half the index. That was mostly Tumblr and Neocities flooding in. By the end that share had dropped to about 12%. Not because I found fewer personal sites. I found more of everything, but the crawl matured into a much broader mix: nonprofits, community sites, software projects, magazines, museums, podcasts.

The nonprofit category alone ended with almost 27,000 real organisations. I spot checked a sample and it’s genuinely full of things like food banks, wildlife charities, and civic groups. That’s the kind of result that makes the weekend feel worth it, a category I barely thought about at the start turning into one of the strongest parts of the index.

Eventually the prioritised categories ran dry and the crawler started clearing the zero-priority backlog, the stuff that had been queued the whole time but never bubbled up. That backlog is a fair cross-section of the raw internet with none of the curation. So right on schedule, once nothing was left to prioritise ahead of it, the model started cataloguing a wave of adult sites.

Roughly 15% of everything crawled ended up as “empty,” meaning the page was either a bare JavaScript shell my simple HTML parser couldn’t see through, or a bot-detection wall. I never built a fallback that actually renders JavaScript, on purpose, since it would have meant running a full browser at scale, which is a different and much more expensive project. Some of the most aesthetically perfect sites for what I was hunting for are sitting in that empty bucket right now, which stings a little, but was the right tradeoff for a weekend budget.

The part that will actually bite you at scale

If you try this yourself, the crawling and the GPU renting are the fun, satisfying parts. The part that quietly becomes a mess is category and tag handling. I let the model invent its own category and tag names freely, on the theory that it would teach me the taxonomy instead of me guessing one upfront. That was the right call for getting started fast. It also means I ended up with 671 distinct categories, many used exactly once, and over 121,000 tags, more than half used only a single time, mostly because the model spells things slightly differently call to call. I wrote a manual merge tool to clean the worst of it up by hand. That does not scale past a hobby project. If you’re building something bigger than a weekend index, decide up front whether you’re going to constrain the model to a fixed list of categories or budget real time for cleanup, because “just let the model freestyle” catches up with you fast.

The other genuine scaling issue is prompt and crawl steering itself. None of the fixes above came from a clever one-shot prompt. They came from watching production data at several points over the weekend and nudging weights, one file, a handful of numbers, based on what the crawl was actually doing. That loop, look at real output, adjust one lever, watch again, did more work than any amount of upfront planning would have.

So, should you build one

If you want a search engine that only returns the kind of thing you actually go looking for, yes, I think this is very doable in a weekend, and cheap enough that the GPU bill isn’t the reason not to try. The rough shape that worked for me: split fetching from summarising so a slow network connection never leaves an expensive GPU idle, weight your crawl queue instead of hard-blocking categories you don’t want yet, cap subdomains instead of banning whole platforms, skip the model entirely on empty or parked pages, and build some kind of automated sink-detector once you’re past the size where you can eyeball the incoming pages yourself.

I’m not planning to host or release my own production database, at least not right now, so I can’t hand you my 560,000 sites directly. But the code is going up as open source, so you can point your own crawl wherever your own curiosity leads.

blocks.html_en: What I was actually trying to build

sentences.en: What I was actually trying to build
sentences.zh: 我实际上想要构建什么

blocks.html_en: Not “index the web.” Just: find people doing stuff, art, code, hardware, poetry, little theatres, and not drown in docs.company.com. Personal, single user, no accounts. A crawler that only ever looks at homepages, a small local language model that reads each one and writes a name, two or three sentences, a category, and a handful of tags. A little search UI on top with fuzzy matching so I could type half a word and still find the right site.

sentences.en: Not “index the web.”
sentences.zh: 不是“索引网络”。

sentences.en: Just: find people doing stuff, art, code, hardware, poetry, little theatres, and not drown in docs.company.com.
sentences.zh: 只是：找到人们做一些事情，艺术、代码、硬件、诗歌、小剧院，而不是淹没在 docs.company.com 中。

sentences.en: Personal, single user, no accounts.
sentences.zh: 个人、单用户、无帐户。

sentences.en: A crawler that only ever looks at homepages, a small local language model that reads each one and writes a name, two or three sentences, a category, and a handful of tags.
sentences.zh: 一个只查看主页的爬虫，一个小型的本地语言模型，可以读取每个页面并写入一个名称、两三个句子、一个类别和一些标签。

sentences.en: A little search UI on top with fuzzy matching so I could type half a word and still find the right site.
sentences.zh: 顶部有一个带有模糊匹配的小搜索用户界面，因此我可以输入半个单词，但仍然可以找到正确的网站。

blocks.html_en: I wrote down what I was explicitly not building, mostly so that agents helping me wouldn’t quietly “simplify” it into something bigger: no IP scanning, no Redis, no storing full page HTML, no recrawl scheduler, nothing multi-tenant. Ignore was just a checkbox on a category, applied at search time. The crawler still summarised ecommerce sites, I just didn’t have to look at them.

sentences.en: I wrote down what I was explicitly not building, mostly so that agents helping me wouldn’t quietly “simplify” it into something bigger: no IP scanning, no Redis, no storing full page HTML, no recrawl scheduler, nothing multi-tenant.
sentences.zh: 我写下了我明确没有构建的内容，主要是为了让帮助我的代理不会悄悄地将其“简化”成更大的东西：没有 IP 扫描，没有 Redis，没有存储整页 HTML，没有重新抓取调度程序，没有多租户。

sentences.en: Ignore was just a checkbox on a category, applied at search time.
sentences.zh: 忽略只是类别上的一个复选框，在搜索时应用。

sentences.en: The crawler still summarised ecommerce sites, I just didn’t have to look at them.
sentences.zh: 爬虫仍然总结了电子商务网站，我只是不必看它们。

blocks.html_en: The napkin math was tens of millions of domains at roughly 1KB of metadata each, which is genuinely nothing for a Postgres box. Page text itself was never meant to be a corpus, just a scratch buffer that gets thrown away the moment the model is done with it.

sentences.en: The napkin math was tens of millions of domains at roughly 1KB of metadata each, which is genuinely nothing for a Postgres box.
sentences.zh: 餐巾纸上的数学计算是数千万个域，每个域大约有 1KB 的元数据，这对于 Postgres 盒子来说确实不算什么。

sentences.en: Page text itself was never meant to be a corpus, just a scratch buffer that gets thrown away the moment the model is done with it.
sentences.zh: 页面文本本身从来就不是一个语料库，只是一个临时缓冲区，模型完成后就会被丢弃。

blocks.html_en: The machine

sentences.en: The machine
sentences.zh: 机器

blocks.html_en: Four processes, three of them on my own PC, one rented GPU that never touches the database directly:

sentences.en: Four processes, three of them on my own PC, one rented GPU that never touches the database directly:
sentences.zh: 四个进程，其中三个在我自己的 PC 上，一个租用的 GPU，从不直接接触数据库：

blocks.html_en: • A fetcher. Grabs a pending domain, tries HTTPS then HTTP, pulls the title, body text, and outbound links with a simple HTML parser, no JavaScript execution. Sets the row to “ready.”

sentences.en: A fetcher.
sentences.zh: 一个拾取器。

sentences.en: Grabs a pending domain, tries HTTPS then HTTP, pulls the title, body text, and outbound links with a simple HTML parser, no JavaScript execution.
sentences.zh: 获取待处理的域，先尝试 HTTPS，然后再尝试 HTTP，使用简单的 HTML 解析器提取标题、正文和出站链接，无需执行 JavaScript。

sentences.en: Sets the row to “ready.”
sentences.zh: 将行设置为“就绪”。

blocks.html_en: • A worker. Grabs a ready domain, skips the model entirely if the page is empty, parked, or a bot-challenge wall, otherwise makes one structured request to a small local model (Gemma, 4B parameters) and gets back a name, summary, category, and tags. Wipes the scratch text, enqueues the outbound links at a priority based on what kind of page they came from.

sentences.en: A worker.
sentences.zh: 一名工人。

sentences.en: Grabs a ready domain, skips the model entirely if the page is empty, parked, or a bot-challenge wall, otherwise makes one structured request to a small local model (Gemma, 4B parameters) and gets back a name, summary, category, and tags.
sentences.zh: 获取一个准备好的域，如果页面为空、停放或有机器人挑战墙，则完全跳过模型，否则向小型本地模型（Gemma、4B 参数）发出一个结构化请求，并获取名称、摘要、类别和标签。

sentences.en: Wipes the scratch text, enqueues the outbound links at a priority based on what kind of page they came from.
sentences.zh: 擦除草稿文本，根据出站链接来自的页面类型优先将其排入队列。

blocks.html_en: • A steward. This one doesn’t touch the main queue at all. It samples domains from hosts that are producing suspiciously many pages, asks the model “block, keep, or unsure,” and quietly maintains a blocklist. More on why I needed this later.

sentences.en: A steward.
sentences.zh: 一个管家。

sentences.en: This one doesn’t touch the main queue at all.
sentences.zh: 这个根本不涉及主队列。

sentences.en: It samples domains from hosts that are producing suspiciously many pages, asks the model “block, keep, or unsure,” and quietly maintains a blocklist.
sentences.zh: 它从产生可疑大量页面的主机中采样域，询问模型“阻止、保留或不确定”，并悄悄地维护一个阻止列表。

sentences.en: More on why I needed this later.
sentences.zh: 稍后会详细说明为什么我需要这个。

blocks.html_en: • An API and a tiny web UI. Search with filters, a page to toggle which categories are hidden, and a dashboard so I could actually see what the factory was doing instead of squinting at logs.

sentences.en: An API and a tiny web UI.
sentences.zh: 一个 API 和一个小型 Web UI。

sentences.en: Search with filters, a page to toggle which categories are hidden, and a dashboard so I could actually see what the factory was doing instead of squinting at logs.
sentences.zh: 使用过滤器进行搜索，一个用于切换隐藏类别的页面，以及一个仪表板，这样我就可以实际看到工厂在做什么，而不是眯着眼睛看日志。

blocks.html_en: Everything the fetcher grabs lives directly on the domain’s own database row while it’s “in progress.” Once the model is done with it, that text gets wiped. That matters more than it sounds, because at any real scale you cannot let raw page text pile up forever. Forty million rows times a few kilobytes each adds up fast, and I only needed that text for the few seconds the model was reading it.

sentences.en: Everything the fetcher grabs lives directly on the domain’s own database row while it’s “in progress.”
sentences.zh: 当“正在进行”时，获取器抓取的所有内容都直接存在于域自己的数据库行中。

sentences.en: Once the model is done with it, that text gets wiped.
sentences.zh: 一旦模型完成，该文本就会被擦除。

sentences.en: That matters more than it sounds, because at any real scale you cannot let raw page text pile up forever.
sentences.zh: 这比听起来更重要，因为在任何实际规模下，您都不能让原始页面文本永远堆积起来。

sentences.en: Forty million rows times a few kilobytes each adds up fast, and I only needed that text for the few seconds the model was reading it.
sentences.zh: 四千万行乘以每行几千字节加起来很快，而且我只需要模型读取该文本的几秒钟。

blocks.html_en: The web is 90% corporate, actually

sentences.en: The web is 90% corporate, actually
sentences.zh: 事实上，网络 90% 都是企业化的

blocks.html_en: The first version worked within a couple hours. Point it at a sample of domains, watch things get summarised, search for them. Great. Then, Sunday afternoon, I looked at what had actually been catalogued and it was the wrong web. Over 90% corporate sites and documentation. My seed list was skewed and the crawler had no opinions about what to chase next.

sentences.en: The first version worked within a couple hours.
sentences.zh: 第一个版本在几个小时内就成功了。

sentences.en: Point it at a sample of domains, watch things get summarised, search for them.
sentences.zh: 将其指向域样本，观察事物的总结，然后搜索它们。

sentences.en: Great.
sentences.zh: 伟大的。

sentences.en: Then, Sunday afternoon, I looked at what had actually been catalogued and it was the wrong web.
sentences.zh: 然后，周日下午，我查看了实际编目的内容，发现这是一个错误的网站。

sentences.en: Over 90% corporate sites and documentation.
sentences.zh: 超过 90% 的公司网站和文档。

sentences.en: My seed list was skewed and the crawler had no opinions about what to chase next.
sentences.zh: 我的种子列表是倾斜的，爬虫对于下一步要追逐什么没有意见。

blocks.html_en: The fix wasn’t to block anything. Blocking felt tempting but wrong, because a boring corporate docs page might still link out to someone’s personal blog, and I didn’t want to lose that. Instead I weighted the queue: pages classified as “portfolio” or “zine” or “software” push their outbound links way up the priority list, pages classified as “corporate” or “docs” push theirs down. One text file, category-priority.txt, became the steering wheel for the rest of the weekend. I’d tune a number, watch what came in over the next hour, tune again.

sentences.en: The fix wasn’t to block anything.
sentences.zh: 解决办法不是阻止任何东西。

sentences.en: Blocking felt tempting but wrong, because a boring corporate docs page might still link out to someone’s personal blog, and I didn’t want to lose that.
sentences.zh: 阻止感觉很诱人，但却是错误的，因为一个无聊的公司文档页面可能仍然链接到某人的个人博客，而我不想失去它。

sentences.en: Instead I weighted the queue: pages classified as “portfolio” or “zine” or “software” push their outbound links way up the priority list, pages classified as “corporate” or “docs” push theirs down.

sentences.en: One text file, category-priority.txt, became the steering wheel for the rest of the weekend.

sentences.en: I’d tune a number, watch what came in over the next hour, tune again.
sentences.zh: 我会调整一个数字，观察接下来一个小时内收到的内容，然后再次调整。

sentences.en: That same afternoon I wiped the database twice because the quality was bad enough to just start over.
sentences.zh: 当天下午，我擦除了数据库两次，因为质量太差，只能重新开始。

sentences.en: Two bugs stood out:
sentences.zh: 有两个错误很突出：

blocks.html_en: One site’s summary field just said “academic-profile,” a category label the model had shoved into the wrong slot. Fix: treat a suspiciously short summary as a failure and retry once with a stricter prompt.

sentences.en: One site’s summary field just said “academic-profile,” a category label the model had shoved into the wrong slot.
sentences.zh: 一个网站的摘要字段只显示“学术概况”，该模型将这一类别标签塞入了错误的位置。

sentences.en: Fix: treat a suspiciously short summary as a failure and retry once with a stricter prompt.
sentences.zh: 修复：将可疑的简短摘要视为失败，并使用更严格的提示重试一次。

blocks.html_en: Another site, a GoDaddy domain-parking page with basically no real HTML, got summarised by the model as being “for the furry community.” but it had just seen the word “furry” in the hostname, with empty body, and invented an entire fandom site out of nothing. That one taught me the actual rule: trust visible text over the title, trust the title over anything guessed from the domain name, and if a page is near-empty or clearly parked, don’t even bother asking the model, just mark it and move on.

sentences.en: Another site, a GoDaddy domain-parking page with basically no real HTML, got summarised by the model as being “for the furry community.”
sentences.zh: 另一个网站是一个基本上没有真正 HTML 的 GoDaddy 域名停放页面，模型将其总结为“针对毛茸茸的社区”。

sentences.en: but it had just seen the word “furry” in the hostname, with empty body, and invented an entire fandom site out of nothing.
sentences.zh: 但它只是在主机名中看到了“毛茸茸的”一词，身体空虚，就凭空发明了一个完整的粉丝网站。

sentences.en: That one taught me the actual rule: trust visible text over the title, trust the title over anything guessed from the domain name, and if a page is near-empty or clearly parked, don’t even bother asking the model, just mark it and move on.
sentences.zh: 那条告诉了我实际的规则：信任可见文本而不是标题，信任标题而不是从域名猜测的任何内容，如果页面接近空或明显停放，甚至不必费心询问模型，只需标记它并继续。

blocks.html_en: Sunday night: Tumblr is not the web

sentences.en: Sunday night: Tumblr is not the web
sentences.zh: 周日晚上：Tumblr 不是网络

blocks.html_en: By evening the crawl had a new problem. Tumblr and Neocities blogs were showing up in such volume that they were going to become the entire index. My first instinct was to block them, which felt wrong, because Neocities specifically is exactly the aesthetic I was hunting for. The actual fix was a cap: allow the main domain always, but once a given root domain has produced more than 100 subdomains, stop enqueueing new ones from it. One pass of that rule deleted over 45,000 queued pages instantly. Tumblr still ended up contributing over 9,000 pages to the final index, since the cap only applies going forward, but it stopped being the whole story.

sentences.en: By evening the crawl had a new problem.
sentences.zh: 到了晚上，爬行又出现了一个新问题。

sentences.en: Tumblr and Neocities blogs were showing up in such volume that they were going to become the entire index.
sentences.zh: Tumblr 和 Neocities 博客的出现量如此之大，以至于它们将成为整个索引。

sentences.en: My first instinct was to block them, which felt wrong, because Neocities specifically is exactly the aesthetic I was hunting for.
sentences.zh: 我的第一反应是阻止它们，但这感觉不对，因为 Neocities 正是我所追求的美学。

sentences.en: The actual fix was a cap: allow the main domain always, but once a given root domain has produced more than 100 subdomains, stop enqueueing new ones from it.
sentences.zh: 实际的修复是一个上限：始终允许主域，但是一旦给定的根域生成了超过 100 个子域，就停止从中排队新的子域。

sentences.en: One pass of that rule deleted over 45,000 queued pages instantly.
sentences.zh: 该规则的一次通过立即删除了超过 45,000 个排队的页面。

sentences.en: Tumblr still ended up contributing over 9,000 pages to the final index, since the cap only applies going forward, but it stopped being the whole story.
sentences.zh: Tumblr 最终仍然为最终索引贡献了 9,000 多个页面，因为上限仅适用于未来，但这不再是故事的全部。

blocks.html_en: This was also the night the actual purpose came into focus, less “index everything,” more “find the people making things for a community.” I reseeded the crawl with about ten deliberately chosen doors: tilde communities, small independent blogging platforms, a webring or two. Almost the entire final index traces back to links found from those ten seeds, not from the seed list itself.

sentences.en: This was also the night the actual purpose came into focus, less “index everything,” more “find the people making things for a community.”
sentences.zh: 这也是真正的目的成为焦点的那天晚上，更少的“索引一切”，更多的“找到为社区创造东西的人”。

sentences.en: I reseeded the crawl with about ten deliberately chosen doors: tilde communities, small independent blogging platforms, a webring or two.
sentences.zh: 我重新播种了大约十个故意选择的门：波浪号社区、小型独立博客平台、一两个网络环。

sentences.en: Almost the entire final index traces back to links found from those ten seeds, not from the seed list itself.
sentences.zh: 几乎整个最终索引都追溯到从这十个种子找到的链接，而不是从种子列表本身。

blocks.html_en: Monday morning brought a related flavor of the same problem: forum farms and Chinese B2B vendor microsites riding a “forum” category boost into a black hole of near-identical pages. Same lesson, different category. I demoted “forum” hard and started keeping an explicit blocklist file for known mills.

sentences.zh: 周一早上，同样的问题也出现了相关的情况：论坛农场和中国 B2B 供应商微型网站凭借“论坛”类别进入了几乎相同页面的黑洞。

sentences.en: Same lesson, different category.
sentences.zh: 同一课，不同类别。

sentences.en: I demoted “forum” hard and started keeping an explicit blocklist file for known mills.
sentences.zh: 我对“论坛”进行了严格降级，并开始为已知工厂保留一个明确的阻止列表文件。

blocks.html_en: Renting a GPU, badly, then well

sentences.en: Renting a GPU, badly, then well
sentences.zh: 租用 GPU，不好，然后好

blocks.html_en: My own GPU, a consumer card, could summarise roughly one page per second running locally. Fine for building the prompt, hopeless for actually filling an index. So I rented a cloud GPU to run the same small model at real concurrency, and this is where most of my actual debugging time went, none of it about the AI itself.

sentences.en: My own GPU, a consumer card, could summarise roughly one page per second running locally.
sentences.zh: 我自己的 GPU（消费卡）可以概括每秒大约本地运行一个页面。

sentences.en: Fine for building the prompt, hopeless for actually filling an index.
sentences.zh: 对于构建提示来说还不错，但对于实际填充索引来说却毫无希望。

sentences.en: So I rented a cloud GPU to run the same small model at real concurrency, and this is where most of my actual debugging time went, none of it about the AI itself.
sentences.zh: 所以我租了一个云 GPU 来以真正的并发速度运行同一个小模型，这就是我大部分实际调试时间都花在哪里的地方，与 AI 本身无关。

blocks.html_en: The short version: my first rental setup used a wrapper library that insisted on spinning up a distributed compute framework even for a single GPU, and that framework fought with the host machine for CPU time. I was paying for a GPU and getting throttled by CPU contention I never asked for. Threw that away, ran the plain open source inference server instead, no wrapper. Hit a crash on cold start at high concurrency, which turned out to be a memory spike during the first batch, not a steady-state problem, fixed by ramping concurrency up gradually instead of slamming it at full speed from a cold start.

sentences.en: The short version: my first rental setup used a wrapper library that insisted on spinning up a distributed compute framework even for a single GPU, and that framework fought with the host machine for CPU time.
sentences.zh: 简而言之：我的第一个租赁设置使用了一个包装器库，即使对于单个 GPU，该库也坚持旋转分布式计算框架，并且该框架与主机争夺 CPU 时间。

sentences.en: I was paying for a GPU and getting throttled by CPU contention I never asked for.
sentences.zh: 我花钱购买了 GPU，但却因我从未要求的 CPU 争用而受到限制。

sentences.en: Threw that away, ran the plain open source inference server instead, no wrapper.
sentences.zh: 把它扔掉，运行普通的开源推理服务器，没有包装器。

sentences.en: Hit a crash on cold start at high concurrency, which turned out to be a memory spike during the first batch, not a steady-state problem, fixed by ramping concurrency up gradually instead of slamming it at full speed from a cold start.
sentences.zh: 高并发冷启动时发生崩溃，结果证明这是第一批期间的内存峰值，而不是稳态问题，通过逐渐增加并发而不是从冷启动全速猛击并发来修复。

blocks.html_en: The machine that actually did the job was a mid-range workstation GPU with a full, unshared set of CPU cores attached. That distinction, a dedicated CPU slice versus an impressively named but shared one, may have mattered more than the GPU model itself. Sustained throughput on that box was around 600 summaries a minute, at a rental cost of about thirty five cents an hour. That’s roughly a dollar to catalogue a hundred thousand sites.

sentences.en: The machine that actually did the job was a mid-range workstation GPU with a full, unshared set of CPU cores attached.
sentences.zh: 实际完成这项工作的机器是一个中档工作站 GPU，附加了一组完整的、非共享的 CPU 核心。

sentences.en: That distinction, a dedicated CPU slice versus an impressively named but shared one, may have mattered more than the GPU model itself.
sentences.zh: 专用 CPU 切片与名称令人印象深刻但共享的 CPU 切片之间的区别可能比 GPU 模型本身更重要。

sentences.en: Sustained throughput on that box was around 600 summaries a minute, at a rental cost of about thirty five cents an hour.
sentences.zh: 该盒子的持续吞吐量约为每分钟 600 个摘要，租金成本约为每小时 35 美分。

sentences.en: That’s roughly a dollar to catalogue a hundred thousand sites.
sentences.zh: 对十万个网站进行编目大约需要一美元。

blocks.html_en: If you try this yourself, the crawling and the GPU renting are the fun, satisfying parts. The part that quietly becomes a mess is category and tag handling. I let the model invent its own category and tag names freely, on the theory that it would teach me the taxonomy instead of me guessing one upfront. That was the right call for getting started fast. content_html_zh:
马林鱼

周日，凌晨 2 点。 我睡不着，又对搜索引擎感到恼火。 我真正关心的每一个查询，作品集、杂志、奇怪的小艺术项目、单人软件，都淹没在一英尺的公司文档和 SEO 污泥之下。 所以我做了你在凌晨 2 点做的事情：我打开一个终端并输入了一个计划。

“我只想为自己制作一个搜索引擎。 有 40 多万个域名。 我们可以存储有关每个的一些元数据。 即使每个 1KB 也是 40GB，这是可行的。”

到周三午餐时，我已经对 560,183 个主页进行了编目，接下来值得获取的内容排空了，我决定停止。 这就是那个周末的故事：我建造了什么，损坏了什么，花费了多少，以及如果你想建造自己的，我会告诉你什么。

标题中，如果您只阅读其中一段：花费大约 10 美元、过夜 GPU 租金以及运行时几个小时的操控，您就可以在磁盘上不到 1GB 的情况下拥有包含数十万个网站的个人搜索索引。 这就是整个球场。 下面的一切都是我如何到达那里以及锋利的边缘在哪里。

完整的技术细节单独提供。

我实际上想要构建什么

不是“索引网络”。 只是：找到人们做一些事情，艺术、代码、硬件、诗歌、小剧院，而不是淹没在 docs.company.com 中。 个人、单用户、无帐户。 一个只查看主页的爬虫，一个小型的本地语言模型，可以读取每个页面并写入一个名称、两三个句子、一个类别和一些标签。 顶部有一个带有模糊匹配的小搜索用户界面，因此我可以输入半个单词，但仍然可以找到正确的网站。

我写下了我明确没有构建的内容，主要是为了让帮助我的代理不会悄悄地将其“简化”成更大的东西：没有 IP 扫描，没有 Redis，没有存储整页 HTML，没有重新抓取调度程序，没有多租户。 忽略只是类别上的一个复选框，在搜索时应用。 爬虫仍然总结了电子商务网站，我只是不必看它们。

餐巾纸上的数学计算是数千万个域，每个域大约有 1KB 的元数据，这对于 Postgres 盒子来说确实不算什么。 页面文本本身从来就不是一个语料库，只是一个临时缓冲区，模型完成后就会被丢弃。

机器

四个进程，其中三个在我自己的 PC 上，一个租用的 GPU，从不直接接触数据库：

  • 一个拾取器。 获取待处理的域，先尝试 HTTPS，然后再尝试 HTTP，使用简单的 HTML 解析器提取标题、正文和出站链接，无需执行 JavaScript。 将行设置为“就绪”。
  • 一名工人。 获取一个准备好的域，如果页面为空、停放或有机器人挑战墙，则完全跳过模型，否则向小型本地模型（Gemma、4B 参数）发出一个结构化请求，并获取名称、摘要、类别和标签。 擦除草稿文本，根据出站链接来自的页面类型优先将其排入队列。
  • 一个管家。 这个根本不涉及主队列。 它从产生可疑大量页面的主机中采样域，询问模型“阻止、保留或不确定”，并悄悄地维护一个阻止列表。 稍后会详细说明为什么我需要这个。
  • 一个 API 和一个小型 Web UI。 使用过滤器进行搜索，一个用于切换隐藏类别的页面，以及一个仪表板，这样我就可以实际看到工厂在做什么，而不是眯着眼睛看日志。

当“正在进行”时，获取器抓取的所有内容都直接存在于域自己的数据库行中。 一旦模型完成，该文本就会被擦除。 这比听起来更重要，因为在任何实际规模下，您都不能让原始页面文本永远堆积起来。 四千万行乘以每行几千字节加起来很快，而且我只需要模型读取该文本的几秒钟。

事实上，网络 90% 都是企业化的

第一个版本在几个小时内就成功了。 将其指向域样本，观察事物的总结，然后搜索它们。 伟大的。 然后，周日下午，我查看了实际编目的内容，发现这是一个错误的网站。 超过 90% 的公司网站和文档。 我的种子列表是倾斜的，爬虫对于下一步要追逐什么没有意见。

解决办法不是阻止任何东西。 阻止感觉很诱人，但却是错误的，因为一个无聊的公司文档页面可能仍然链接到某人的个人博客，而我不想失去它。 相反，我对队列进行了加权：分类为“投资组合”或“杂志”或“软件”的页面将其出站链接推到优先级列表的上方，分类为“公司”或“文档”的页面将其出站链接推低。 一个文本文件，category-priority.txt，成为周末剩余时间的方向盘。 我会调整一个数字，观察接下来一个小时内收到的内容，然后再次调整。

当天下午，我擦除了数据库两次，因为质量太差，只能重新开始。 有两个错误很突出：

一个网站的摘要字段只显示“学术概况”，该模型将这一类别标签塞入了错误的位置。 修复：将可疑的简短摘要视为失败，并使用更严格的提示重试一次。

另一个网站是一个基本上没有真正 HTML 的 GoDaddy 域名停放页面，模型将其总结为“针对毛茸茸的社区”。 但它只是在主机名中看到了“毛茸茸的”一词，身体空虚，就凭空发明了一个完整的粉丝网站。 那条告诉了我实际的规则：信任可见文本而不是标题，信任标题而不是从域名猜测的任何内容，如果页面接近空或明显停放，甚至不必费心询问模型，只需标记它并继续。

周日晚上：Tumblr 不是网络

到了晚上，爬行又出现了一个新问题。 Tumblr 和 Neocities 博客的出现量如此之大，以至于它们将成为整个索引。 我的第一反应是阻止它们，但这感觉不对，因为 Neocities 正是我所追求的美学。 实际的修复是一个上限：始终允许主域，但是一旦给定的根域生成了超过 100 个子域，就停止从中排队新的子域。 该规则的一次通过立即删除了超过 45,000 个排队的页面。 Tumblr 最终仍然为最终索引贡献了 9,000 多个页面，因为上限仅适用于未来，但这不再是故事的全部。

这也是真正的目的成为焦点的那天晚上，更少的“索引一切”，更多的“找到为社区创造东西的人”。 我重新播种了大约十个故意选择的门：波浪号社区、小型独立博客平台、一两个网络环。 几乎整个最终索引都追溯到从这十个种子找到的链接，而不是从种子列表本身。

周一早上，同样的问题也出现了相关的情况：论坛农场和中国 B2B 供应商微型网站凭借“论坛”类别进入了几乎相同页面的黑洞。 同一课，不同类别。 我对“论坛”进行了严格降级，并开始为已知工厂保留一个明确的阻止列表文件。

租用 GPU，不好，然后好

我自己的 GPU（消费卡）可以概括每秒大约本地运行一个页面。 对于构建提示来说还不错，但对于实际填充索引来说却毫无希望。 所以我租了一个云 GPU 来以真正的并发速度运行同一个小模型，这就是我大部分实际调试时间都花在哪里的地方，与 AI 本身无关。

简而言之：我的第一个租赁设置使用了一个包装器库，即使对于单个 GPU，该库也坚持旋转分布式计算框架，并且该框架与主机争夺 CPU 时间。 我花钱购买了 GPU，但却因我从未要求的 CPU 争用而受到限制。 把它扔掉，运行普通的开源推理服务器，没有包装器。 高并发冷启动时发生崩溃，结果证明这是第一批期间的内存峰值，而不是稳态问题，通过逐渐增加并发而不是从冷启动全速猛击并发来修复。

实际完成这项工作的机器是一个中档工作站 GPU，附加了一组完整的、非共享的 CPU 核心。 专用 CPU 切片与名称令人印象深刻但共享的 CPU 切片之间的区别可能比 GPU 模型本身更重要。 该盒子的持续吞吐量约为每分钟 600 个摘要，租金成本约为每小时 35 美分。 对十万个网站进行编目大约需要一美元。

以这些速率进行大致计算，假设您可以保持 GPU 供电并且它们大致呈线性扩展。 对于给定的里程碑，租用两到三个 GPU 的成本大致相同，因为每个 GPU 的运行时间都更少；您大多是几天前购买的：

午夜发明第二个工人

周一深夜，盯着仍在运行的爬行，我问自己这样的问题：在这种规模下，我无法手动观察不良螺旋，我是否可以从任何产生可疑多的域中获得第二个小流程样本，五个，然后十个完整页面，并询问模型本身是否阻止它？

他成为了管家，正是这个单一的补充让索引从大约 65,000 页增长到 560,000 页，而无需我来照管。 它位于我用于快速工作的同一张本地卡和 LM Studio 上，因此螺旋判断永远不会与填充索引的租用 GPU 竞争。 在运行过程中，它自己屏蔽了 177 个问题域，几乎全部是酒店和预订工厂，并且正确地保留了诸如大学和合法大型平台之类恰好有很多子域的东西。

这些数字实际上是什么样的

在四天的时间里观看这确实是有趣的部分。 早期，博客和个人网站占据了索引的一半以上。 其中大部分是 Tumblr 和 Neocities 涌入的。 到最后，这一比例已降至 12% 左右。 并不是因为我发现的个人网站较少。 我发现了更多的东西，但爬行逐渐成熟为更广泛的组合：非营利组织、社区网站、软件项目、杂志、博物馆、播客。

仅非营利组织类别就有近 27,000 个真实组织。 我抽查了一个样本，里面确实充满了诸如食品银行、野生动物慈善机构和民间团体之类的东西。 这样的结果让周末感觉值得，我一开始几乎没有想到这一类别变成了该指数中最强的部分之一。

最终，优先类别耗尽，爬虫开始清除零优先级的积压工作，这些工作一直在排队，但从未出现过。 该待办事项是原始互联网的一个公平的横截面，没有任何管理。 因此，正如计划一样，一旦没有什么可以优先考虑的事情，该模型就开始对一系列成人网站进行编目。

大约 15% 的爬行内容最终都是“空的”，这意味着该页面要么是我的简单 HTML 解析器无法看穿的裸露 JavaScript shell，要么是机器人检测墙。 我从来没有故意构建一个实际渲染 JavaScript 的后备方案，因为这意味着大规模运行一个完整的浏览器，这是一个不同且昂贵得多的项目。 我正在寻找的一些最美观完美的网站现在就坐在那个空桶里，这有点刺痛，但对于周末预算来说是正确的权衡。

真正会大规模咬你的部分

如果你自己尝试一下，爬行和 GPU 租用是有趣且令人满意的部分。 悄然变得混乱的部分是类别和标签处理。 我让模型自由地发明自己的类别和标签名称，理论上它会教我分类法，而不是我预先猜测。 这是快速开始的正确呼吁。 这也意味着我最终得到了 671 个不同的类别，其中许多仅使用了一次，以及超过 121,000 个标签，其中一半以上仅使用了一次，主要是因为模型对 call 与 call 的拼写略有不同。 我编写了一个手动合并工具来手动清理其中最糟糕的部分。 这并没有超出一个业余爱好项目的范围。 如果您正在构建比周末索引更大的东西，请预先决定是将模型限制在固定的类别列表中还是实时预算以进行清理，因为“让模型自由式”很快就能赶上您。

另一个真正的缩放问题是快速和爬行转向本身。 上述所有修复都不是来自巧妙的一次性提示。 他们在周末的几个时间点观察生产数据，并根据爬行的实际情况微调权重、一个文件、一些数字。 这个循环，查看实际输出，调整一个杠杆，再次观察，比任何数量的前期计划都完成了更多的工作。

那么，您是否应该构建一个

如果你想要一个只返回你实际要寻找的东西的搜索引擎，是的，我认为这在周末是非常可行的，而且足够便宜，GPU 费用并不是不尝试的理由。 对我有用的大致形状是：将提取与汇总分开，这样缓慢的网络连接就不会导致昂贵的 GPU 空闲，对爬行队列进行加权，而不是硬阻止您不想要的类别，限制子域而不是禁止整个平台，完全跳过空白或停放页面上的模型，并在超过可以自己查看传入页面的大小时构建某种自动接收器检测器。

我不打算托管或发布自己的生产数据库，至少现在不打算，所以我不能直接向您提供我的 560,000 个站点。 但代码将作为开源代码发布，因此您可以根据自己的好奇心将自己的爬行指向任何地方。
